summary: Sets out requirements for an Internet audio codec, covering quality, sampling rate, bit rate, and robustness to packet loss, as well as other useful properties. It is informational and fed into later codec work.

plainLanguage.summary: Different kinds of audio need different codecs. A phone call can wait a few tens of milliseconds; playing music together over the network cannot. This memo lists what each application needs from a codec, and the rules a codec must follow to survive the Internet, where packets get lost and the bandwidth changes.

subtitle: The checklist an audio codec has to meet to work well for calls, conferences, games and music over the Internet.

tldr.problem: An audio codec used over the Internet has to cope with lost packets, a network with no guaranteed bandwidth, and several kinds of application that want very different things from it.
tldr.mechanism: The document works from the applications backwards, deriving for each one the delay, bit rate and quality it needs, then collects the constraints the Internet imposes and the detailed requirements that follow from them.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a specification: it names the sampling rates, bit-rate ranges, loss tolerance and processing budgets that a codec is expected to meet.

sections.title: What the Document Is and What Its Terms Mean
sections.content:
The document provides requirements for an audio codec designed specifically for use over the Internet. The requirements attempt to address the needs of the most common Internet interactive audio transmission applications and ensure good quality when operating in conditions that are typical for the Internet. They address quality, sampling rate, delay, bit-rate and packet-loss robustness, and other desirable codec properties are considered as well.

The conventions used for sampling rates are: narrowband is 8 kilohertz, wideband is 16 kHz, super-wideband is 24 or 32 kHz, and full-band is 44.1 or 48 kHz. Codec bit-rates in bits per second are considered without counting any overhead such as IP, UDP and RTP headers or padding. The codec delay is the total algorithmic delay when the codec frame size is added to the look-ahead, and is thus the minimum theoretically achievable end-to-end delay of a transmission system that uses the codec.
sections.plainLanguage: The document uses four width bands for audio, from narrowband telephone speech at 8 kHz up to full-band audio at 44.1 or 48 kHz, which is studio quality. All the bit-rate figures are for the audio itself, with the network overhead left out, and the delay figure is the smallest delay the codec alone can achieve.

sections.title: The Applications and What Each One Needs
sections.content:
For point-to-point calls, which are voice over IP calls between two phones implemented in hardware or software, a wideband codec is required along with narrowband support for compatibility with the public switched telephone network. The range of useful bit-rates is expected to be 12 to 32 kilobits per second for wideband speech and 8 to 16 kbit/s for narrowband speech. The codec delay must be less than 40 milliseconds, but no more than 25 ms is desirable. Support for encoding music is not required, but it is desirable for the codec not to make background music excessively unpleasant to hear, and the codec should be robust to noise even at lower bit-rates.

Conferencing applications have additional requirements on top of those for point-to-point calls. Conferencing systems often have higher-fidelity audio equipment and greater network bandwidth available, especially when video transmission is involved, so support for super-wideband audio becomes important, with useful bit-rates in the 32 to 64 kbit/s range. The ability to vary the bit-rate according to the difficulty of the audio signal is desirable. Conferencing end-points often operate in hands-free conditions, which creates acoustic echo problems, so lower delay is important as it reduces the quality degradation due to any residual echo after acoustic echo cancellation; the codec delay must be less than 30 ms, and an optional low-delay mode with less than 10 ms delay is desirable. Because a bridge mixes some or all of the streams and sends them back, it is important that the codec not produce annoying artifacts when two voices are present at the same time, and that the mixing be easy to perform. To make it easier to determine which streams have to be mixed, it must be possible to measure or estimate the voice activity in a packet without having to fully decode it.

Most telepresence applications are essentially very high-quality video-conferencing environments, so all the conferencing requirements also apply, and they additionally require super-wideband and full-band audio capability with useful bit-rates in the 32 to 80 kbit/s range. Most require more than one audio channel, so support for stereo and multi-channel is important.

Teleoperation applications are similar to telepresence but involve remote physical interaction, such as controlling a robot while receiving real-time audio feedback from it, and for these the delay has to be less than 10 ms. The requirements for remote software services, including remote desktop applications, remote virtualization and interactive media rendered remotely, are similar, and full-band audio with an algorithmic delay below 10 ms is important.

In-game voice chat is similar to conferencing, with the main difference being that narrowband compatibility is not necessary. While for most applications a codec delay up to 30 ms is acceptable, a low-delay option of less than 10 ms is highly desirable, especially for games with rapid interactions, and the ability to use variable bit-rate with a maximum allowed bit-rate is highly desirable because it can significantly reduce the bandwidth requirement for a game server.

Live music over the Internet is one of the most demanding applications, requiring extremely low end-to-end delay. For most scenarios, total end-to-end delays up to 25 ms could be tolerated by musicians, with the absolute limit where none of the scenarios are possible being around 50 ms. To achieve this on the Internet, whether in the same city or a nearby one, the network propagation time must be taken into account, and after subtracting the delay of the audio buffer, jitter buffer and acoustic path, that leaves around 2 ms to 10 ms for the total delay of the codec. Considering the speed of light in fiber, every 1 ms reduction in the codec delay increases the range over which synchronization is possible by approximately 200 km. Because the music quality requirements essentially forbid the use of a non-linear processor with acoustic echo cancellation, echo is an even more important issue for network music than for conferencing. The full audio bandwidth must be transmitted with a bit-rate sufficient to provide near-transparent to transparent quality, which with current audio coding technology corresponds to approximately 64 to 128 kbit/s per channel.
sections.plainLanguage: The applications differ mostly in how much delay they can put up with. A call can wait forty milliseconds and a conference under thirty, but playing music together needs the codec itself to add no more than about ten. Musicians will tolerate about twenty-five milliseconds end to end, and every millisecond the codec saves adds roughly two hundred kilometres of distance over which players can stay together.

sections.title: What the Internet Imposes on the Codec
sections.content:
Packet losses are inevitable on the Internet, and dealing with them is one of the most fundamental requirements for an Internet audio codec. While any audio codec can be combined with a good packet-loss concealment algorithm, the important aspect is what happens on the first packets received after the loss. It should be possible to interpret the contents of any received packet, irrespective of previous losses, as specified in BCP 36, and the decoder should re-synchronize as quickly as possible, so that the output quickly converges to the output that would have been obtained if no loss had occurred.

The constraint of being able to decode any packet has two consequences. The size of a compressed frame must be kept smaller than the maximum transmission unit to avoid fragmentation, and the interpretation of any parameter encoded in the bit-stream must not depend on information contained in other packets. For example, it is not acceptable for a codec to allow signalling a mode change in one packet and assume that subsequent frames will be decoded according to that mode. Although the interpretation of parameters cannot depend on other packets, it is still reasonable to use some amount of prediction across frames, provided that the predictors can resynchronize quickly in case of a lost packet, and it is a desirable property for the codec to allow some real-time control of that trade-off.

To improve robustness to packet loss, it would be desirable for the codec to allow an adaptive amount of side information, for example the retransmission of certain parameters encoded in previous frames. To ensure freedom of implementation, decoder-side-only error concealment does not need to be specified, although a functional algorithm is desirable as part of the codec reference implementation, and any information signalled in the bit-stream intended to aid concealment needs to be specified.

Another important property of the Internet is that it is mostly a best-effort network with no guaranteed bandwidth. The codec has to be able to vary its output bit-rate dynamically, in real time, without requiring an out-of-band signalling mechanism, and without causing audible artifacts at the bit-rate change boundaries. Desirable features include the possibility of smooth bit-rate changes with one byte per frame resolution, and the ability to adapt the bit-rate based on the source signal being encoded, to maximize quality for a certain average bit-rate. Because the Internet transmits data in bytes, a codec should produce compressed data in integer numbers of bytes, and the codec design should take explicit congestion notification into consideration.

Finally, it is important for the resulting codec to be easy to use with the application-layer protocols the IETF has defined for real-time transport of multimedia data. It must be possible to create an RTP payload format that conforms to BCP 36, and if codec parameters need to be negotiated between end-points, the negotiation should be as easy as possible to carry over session initiation protocol and session description protocol, or alternatively over extensible messaging and presence protocol and Jingle.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet loses packets and offers no guaranteed bandwidth, so two rules follow. Every packet must be decodable on its own, because the one before it may never arrive; that means a mode change cannot be signalled in one packet and assumed in the next. And the bit-rate has to be able to move at any moment, without an out-of-band conversation and without a click in the audio.

sections.title: The Detailed Requirements
sections.content:
The operating space for the target applications can be divided in terms of delay: most applications require a medium delay of 20 to 30 ms, while a few require a very low delay of less than 10 ms. It makes sense to divide the space based on delay because lowering the delay has a cost in terms of quality against bit-rate. For medium delay, the codec must be able to operate efficiently within a range of bit-rates per channel of 8 to 16 kbit/s for narrowband, 12 to 32 kbit/s for wideband, 24 to 64 kbit/s for super-wideband and 32 to 80 kbit/s for full-band. A lower-delay codec that can operate in the same range is also acceptable. For very low delay, the codec will need to operate within 32 to 80 kbit/s for super-wideband and 48 to 128 kbit/s for full-band; narrowband and wideband are not required.

Quality is directly linked to bit-rate, so the two must be considered jointly. When comparing bit-rates, the overhead of the IP, UDP and RTP headers should not be considered, but any additional bits required in the RTP payload format after the header should be. The codec to be developed must be better than the generally considered royalty-free codecs: Speex and the internet low bit-rate codec for narrowband, Speex and G.722.1 for wideband, and G.722.1C for super-wideband and full-band. The codecs with additional licensing restrictions should still not be significantly worse, and a desirable objective is that quality be no worse than Adaptive Multi-Rate and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband. Quality should be measured for multiple languages, including tonal languages, and the case of multiple simultaneous voices should be evaluated as well. If a much lower delay is required, the bit-rate for a given quality may be higher than that of the referenced codecs, but in that case the increase in bit-rate must be less than the ratio between the delays.

Robustness to packet loss is a very important aspect of any codec used on the Internet. Codecs must maintain acceptable quality at loss rates up to 5% and maintain good intelligibility up to a 15% loss rate. At any sampling rate, bit-rate and packet-loss rate, the quality must be no less than that obtained with the Speex codec or the GSM-FR codec in the same conditions. The actual packet-loss patterns used in testing must be obtained from real packet-loss traces collected on the Internet rather than from loss models, and should be representative of the typical environments in which the applications operate.

The codec should be implementable on a wide range of devices, so there should be a fixed-point implementation or at least assurance that a reasonable one is possible. The computational resources figures are upper bounds: narrowband 40 MHz, which is 2% of a 2 GHz CPU core, wideband 80 MHz, 4% of a core, and super-wideband and full-band 200 MHz, 10% of a core. For applications that require mixing, it should be possible to estimate the energy and voice activity status of the decoded signal with less than 10% of those complexity figures. The reference implementation must not depend on special hardware features, and the codec context and state size required should be no more than twice the sampling rate times the number of channels in bytes in floating point, and less than that in fixed point.
sections.plainLanguage: The bit-rate ranges are set per bandwidth band, with one table for the ordinary delay most applications tolerate and one for the very low delay that teleoperation needs. Quality has to beat the royalty-free codecs already in use, and the loss tolerance is explicit: five percent loss may still be acceptable, fifteen percent must still be intelligible. The processing budget is small enough to run on a phone.

sections.title: Additional Considerations and Security
sections.content:
There are additional features or characteristics that may be desirable under some circumstances, but should not be part of the strict requirements; the benefit of meeting them should be weighed against the associated cost.

Low-complexity audio mixing matters in applications with a mixing server such as conferencing and games, where the cost of mixing should be less than decoding all the streams, mixing them and re-encoding. Properties that reduce it include the ability to derive enough parameters, such as loudness or spectral envelope, to estimate voice activity without fully decoding a frame, the ability to mix streams in an intermediate representation such as the transform domain, and the use of bit-stream layers by aggregating a small number of active streams at lower quality.

A layered codec makes it possible to transmit only a subset of the bits and still obtain a valid bit-stream with the quality that would have been obtained by encoding at the corresponding rate, which can be desirable where a mixing server must handle a large number of streams with limited resources. Partial redundancy within packets is another way of increasing robustness to packet loss, by including the base layer of the previous frame or other parameters from previous frames to help the concealment algorithm; it is desirable provided it can be turned on and off dynamically so that no bandwidth is wasted when there is no loss. Stereo support is highly desirable: at a minimum the codec should encode two channels independently without significant stereo image artifacts, and it is desirable to take advantage of the inter-channel redundancy to reduce the bit-rate of stereo audio compared to coding the channels independently.

Most Internet applications do not need to be robust to bit errors, because packets either arrive unaltered or do not arrive at all, so the emphasis should be on packet-loss robustness. That said, extra robustness to bit errors can often be achieved at no cost at all, and robustness to packet loss should never be sacrificed to achieve it. It is desirable for the reference implementation to provide time stretching and shortening, since adaptive jitter buffers often need the audio signal to be stretched or shortened, and doing this inside the decoder is often more efficient than doing it on the decoder's output. The systems providing input to the encoder may be far from ideal, so codecs should be tested to ensure they degrade gracefully under adverse conditions such as tandeming, transcoding, low-quality resampling and digital clipping. Because emergency calls can be analyzed using audio forensics, the encoder must allow discontinuous transmission to be disabled when required. Finally, in order to create the best possible codec for the Internet, there is no requirement for compatibility with legacy Internet codecs.

On security, as for any protocol used over the Internet, avoiding buffer overflows and similar attacks is important, and one very important aspect is to make sure that decoders have a bounded and reasonable worst-case complexity, so that an attacker cannot cause a denial of service by sending packets crafted to take a very long or infinite time to decode. A more subtle aspect is the information leak that can occur when the codec is used over an encrypted channel: it was suggested that use of source-controlled variable bit-rate may reveal some information about a conversation through the size of the compressed packets, so it should be possible to use the codec at a truly constant bit-rate if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The optional extras are mostly about cost and privacy. A mixing server should not have to decode everything it forwards, so the codec should let the server work from a summary of each frame. And because the size of the compressed packets can give away what was said, there has to be a way to force a constant bit-rate when the conversation needs to stay private.

THE RULES THE INTERNET FORCES ON THE BIT-STREAM

items.title: Every packet stands alone
items.text: Any packet must be decodable whatever was lost before it, and the decoder must resynchronize quickly.

items.title: A frame fits in one packet
items.text: The compressed frame must be smaller than the maximum transmission unit, so it is never fragmented.

items.title: No dependence on other packets
items.text: A parameter must not mean something different depending on a packet that may have been lost.

items.title: The bit-rate can move at any time
items.text: It changes in real time, with no out-of-band signalling and no audible click at the boundary.

items.title: Whole bytes
items.text: Compressed data comes out in integer numbers of bytes, since that is what the Internet carries.
